lesson.arabic-classical-register.title_en: Classical Arabic: نَثْر, شِعْر, and words whose meaning has moved
lesson.arabic-classical-register.family_en: What carries over from modern Fuṣḥā, and what an older text can mean differently

table.en: a train; once, a line of camels
a newspaper; once, a palm branch stripped of its leaves
a telephone; once, a voice heard from someone unseen

steps: Classical texts share most of their grammar with modern Fuṣḥā, but their words, genres and habits differ from period to period.
A word can carry an older sense: قِطَار, a train today, was once a line of camels; جَرِيدَة, a newspaper, was a palm branch stripped of its leaves.
So note when and what kind of text it is, and look the word up in a dictionary that covers that period.
Classical prose and poetry each have their own conventions: don't read one as if it were the other.

examples.en: The line of camels moved through the desert.
I took the train to the city.
I read the news item in the newspaper.

why.q_en: How do you know which sense a word has in an old text?
why.a_en: From the text's period and its context: a line about camels in the desert can't mean a train. When in doubt, check a historical dictionary, and keep both senses in your notes until the context settles it.

selftest.why_en: Its modern sense, a train, came later.

selftest.q_en: A word in an old text has a familiar modern meaning. What do you check?
selftest.why_en: An older text may use an older sense.

leads_to.en: Checking an old sense in a historical dictionary.

lesson.arabic-classical-parsing.title_en: Iʿrāb: endings that show who did what
lesson.arabic-classical-parsing.family_en: Parsing a sentence: each word's job, its ending, and what governs it

table.en: the word that governs an ending

steps: الْإِعْرَاب is both the endings and the analysis of them: what each word's job is, and what governs its ending.
Start with the structure: the verb, who does it, to what, and what's attached. Then read the endings.
The endings, not the order, show the roles: in أَكْرَمَ الضَّيْفَ صَاحِبُ الْبَيْتِ, the host honoured the guest: the doer comes last.
Parse to settle a real question of meaning. If two analyses both fit, note both, and check a commentary or a teacher.

examples.en: The poet wrote a letter to his friend.

why.q_en: In أَكْرَمَ الضَّيْفَ صَاحِبُ الْبَيْتِ, how do you know who honoured whom?
why.a_en: From the endings: الضَّيْفَ ends in -a, so it's the object; صَاحِبُ ends in -u, so it's the doer, even though it comes last. Arabic can move words for emphasis because the endings keep the roles.

selftest.q_en: In a verbal sentence, which ending marks the direct object?

choices: the case endings, and parsing them
selftest.answer: the case endings, and parsing them
selftest.why_en: It names both the endings and their analysis.

selftest.q_en: In أَكْرَمَ الضَّيْفَ صَاحِبُ الْبَيْتِ, who is the doer?
selftest.why_en: Its -u marks the doer, though it comes last.

lesson.arabic-historical-lexicon.title_en: Old dictionaries and small words: مُعْجَم, شَاهِد, مَا
lesson.arabic-historical-lexicon.family_en: Using a historical dictionary, and the several jobs of a small word
steps: A historical dictionary gives a word's senses with شَوَاهِد, dated quotations. The earliest one shows the word was in use by then, not that it began then.
Look a word up under its root: the مَادَّة, the entry, gathers its related forms.
Small words have several jobs. مَا can mean "not", "what?" or "what" in the sense of "that which", and the sentence decides: مَا رَأَيْتُهُ, I didn't see him; مَا هَذَا؟, what's this?
Don't read a later, technical sense back into an older text: check the sense against the passage.

examples.en: I looked the word up in the dictionary.
I haven't seen him for a year.

why.q_en: How can مَا mean both "not" and "what"?
why.a_en: They're different uses of one small word, and grammar names each: مَا النَّافِيَةُ, which negates what follows it; مَا الِاسْتِفْهَامِيَّةُ, which asks; and مَا الْمَوْصُولَةُ, "that which". Its place and the rest of the sentence show which it is.

selftest.q_en: In مَا رَأَيْتُهُ, what does مَا do?
selftest.why_en: Before a past verb, it denies it: I didn't see him.

selftest.q_en: What is a شَاهِد in a dictionary?
selftest.why_en: It shows the word in use.

selftest.q_en: A dictionary's earliest quotation for a word is from a certain year. What does that show?
choices: that the word was in use by then
that the word began that year
selftest.answer: that the word was in use by then
selftest.why_en: It may be older than its first recorded example.

lesson.arabic-edition-commentary.title_en: Editions and commentary: تَحْقِيق, مُحَقِّق, شَرْح
lesson.arabic-edition-commentary.family_en: The words for editions, copies and commentary, and keeping the text apart from the notes

table.en: a critical edition, editing a text

steps: Editions can differ in wording, punctuation and vowel marks: note which edition, and which مُحَقِّق, editor, you used.
Keep the text apart from the شَرْح, the commentary, and from the هَامِش, the editor's notes: they explain the text, but they aren't the author's words.
Where copies differ, the editor notes the اِخْتِلَافُ النُّسَخِ, the variants. Read them before you decide a reading is obvious.
A digital copy can carry typing errors: check a page image when the exact wording matters.

examples.en: The editor relied on three copies.
The commentator gave two views on the meaning.
In the margin there's a correction by the editor.

words.en: from, by (-a before the next word)

why.q_en: Why تَحْقِيق, from حَقَّقَ, to verify, for editing a text?
why.a_en: Editing an old text means checking it: comparing the copies, settling the wording and noting where they differ. The editor is the مُحَقِّق, the one who verifies.

selftest.why_en: The one who writes it is a شَارِح.
نُسَخ is the plural of نُسْخَة, a copy.

leads_to.en: Writing your own notes on a short passage.

lesson.arabic-classical-commentary.title_en: Annotating a passage: تَعْلِيق, يَعُودُ الضَّمِيرُ عَلَى
lesson.arabic-classical-commentary.family_en: Notes that solve real difficulties, and saying what a pronoun refers to
steps: Choose a short passage, and write one تَعْلِيق, note, for each real difficulty: a word, a construction, a reference.
Say what a pronoun refers to: يَعُودُ الضَّمِيرُ عَلَى الثَّعْلَبِ, the pronoun refers to the fox. It can change who does the next thing.
Keep the text, your translation and your notes apart, and mark which readings are sure and which are only likelier.
Name the dictionary or commentary each note relies on, and add no motive or moral the text doesn't support.

examples.ar: يَعُودُ الضَّمِيرُ عَلَى الثَّعْلَبِ لَا عَلَى الْأَسَدِ.
examples.en: The pronoun refers to the fox, not the lion.
This is the likelier reading, not a certain one.

examples.ar: كَتَبْتُ تَعْلِيقًا قَصِيرًا عَلَى كُلِّ صُعُوبَةٍ.
examples.en: I wrote a short note on each difficulty.

why.q_en: Why يَعُودُ عَلَى, literally "returns to", for "refers to"?
why.a_en: A pronoun points back to something already named, so grammar says it "returns" to it: يَعُودُ الضَّمِيرُ عَلَى الثَّعْلَبِ. Finding where it returns often settles who did what.

selftest.q_en: What does يَعُودُ الضَّمِيرُ عَلَى mean?
selftest.why_en: It points back to something already named.
From رَجَّحَ, to judge more likely.
